We systematically compare training-free verbalized, token-level and semantic uncertainty estimation methods on twelve MLLMs and five VQA benchmarks. We find that answer length decides which family wins: token-level entropy on short answers, verbalized methods on sentence-length responses, and semantic methods on long-form generation. Token-level entropy becomes far more informative when estimated at a higher temperature than the low ones used to generate answers, and asking a model to judge its own answer becomes more reliable with model size. Building on this, a length-aware recipe that additionally flags responses on which the model abstains outperforms every individual method on average at about a quarter of the cost of semantic methods, although no method attains the coverage required for safe deployment. These results provide practitioners with principled guidance for selecting estimators by answer length and model scale.

authors: Yiqian Yang,Yiqun Duan,Chenyu Liu,Yiqi Wang,Xinliang Zhou,Chin-Teng Lin,Yu Zhang
title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Paradigms, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived paradigms to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange.

authors: Husein Zolkepli
title: How to Reduce Whisper Hallucination
abstract: Whisper is still what runs in production: one permissively licensed checkpoint, 99 languages, no per-language tuning. But it writes sentences nobody said. On 42 clips of pure room tone, whisper-large-v3 emits words on 61.9% of them and emits something on 100%. The usual response is to distil a student from Whisper pseudo-labels, filtering the hallucinations out of the corpus first, which deletes the evidence while leaving the behaviour in place: the student is fitted to the subset where the teacher was right, and inherits a failure mode absent from its own training data. The second response, adding non-speech audio so the model learns to stay quiet, already ships and works, but teaches suppression without discrimination. The checkpoint best on every non-speech arm here is also the one that recovers the fewest genuinely spoken phrases and deletes 58% of repeated speech. The teacher has to be fixed, with both halves of the signal. Our benchmark scores both at once: 11,852 clips over eight arms, 6,267 synthetic positives, 8,296 clips of real audio that made a production model fail, and FLEURS in 58 languages. We collect 40,891 hallucination phrases in 100 languages, choose a text-to-speech system by measurement, and synthesise those phrases as positives, so the model meets the same text both as something to suppress and as something to transcribe. Across 33 matched pairs of fine-tunes differing only by those positives, adding them lowers word emission on real voice-free audio in 31 pairs and raises phrase recovery in 32; among the 30 pairs that hold English accuracy it is 30 out of 30. The best checkpoint takes hallucination on silence from 61.9% to 2.4% and words over real voice-free audio from 99.9% to 47.8%, while raising phrase recovery from 69.8% to 82.7%. The benchmark, lexicon and synthetic corpus are released atthis https URL

authors: Xinghao Chen,Junnan Dong,Cai Ke,Chak Tou Leong,Haocheng Sun,Keyu Chen,Siyu An,Ruizhi Qiao,Xing Sun,Wenjie Li,Xiaoyu Shen
title: ATTUNER: Recomputation-Free Agentic Context KV Reuse
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents repeatedly load reusable content, such as skills, documents, and memory entries, into the current context. Re-encoding this content for every request wastes computation. Position-independent caching (PIC) alleviates this by encoding each artifact independently and reusing its key-value (KV) states at arbitrary positions, but it incurs a quality loss relative to full-context prefill. Existing methods repair this loss by restoring global position IDs or recomputing selected tokens. In this work, we isolate the source of the loss, finding that the positional mismatch has minor effect, and independently cached artifacts retain faithful representations: reading a provided artifact stays largely accurate, and performance degrades only when the model must select among multiple artifacts. Moreover, replacing PIC's attention scores with full-prefill scores recovers performance with the cached KV unchanged, localizing the failure to the attention rather than KV recomputation. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{Attuner}, a query-side adaptation method that learns to read a frozen artifact cache. \textsc{Attuner} inserts low-rank adapters into the query projections and is trained by distilling full-prefill distribution into the student. It trains fewer than 0.05\% of the model parameters and, at inference, requires neither cache recomputation nor a full-context reference. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks covering skills, documents, memory, and code, \textsc{Attuner} substantially outperforms prior PIC baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, matches full-context prefill quality while providing up to $3.73\times$ speedup.

authors: Chahat Raj,Sina Mansouri,Aylin Caliskan,Antonios Anastasopoulos,Ziwei Zhu
title: Debias It Yourself: Teaching LLMs Cognitive Bias Mitigation Interventions
abstract: Bias has long been studied in social psychology and cognitive science, where decades of research have produced a body of validated interventions that reduce stereotypical thinking and prejudiced responses in humans. We propose Debias It Yourself (DIY), a cognitively grounded framework that translates five such interventions into debiasing procedures for large language models and delivers them through three established paradigms: Show (in-context examples), Train (instruction tuning), and Revise (guided self-revision). Across three models, five bias benchmarks, eleven debiasing baselines, and three reasoning benchmarks, Train+Revise and Revise alone attain the top two average ranks, lead the bias-reasoning tradeoff (mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy), and reduce bias on unseen dimensions by up to 14.8%. Our code and data are publicly available.

authors: Yuxiang Wang,Kunyu Feng,Yuancheng Wang,Zihang Liu,Shengbo Cai,Qinke Ni,Wan Lin,Tao Feng,Yingda shen,Ming-Hao Hsu,Zhixian Zhao,Liqiang Zhang,Teddy Sun,Steve Yves,Zhizheng Wu
title: AURAL: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Joint Chunk for Speech Language Models
abstract: Model intelligence and fast response jointly shape the quality of interaction with speech language models, yet remain difficult to achieve together. Explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning and audio understanding, but generating intermediate reasoning tokens delays responses. Describing fine-grained acoustic cues further lengthens CoT and increases latency. Latent reasoning can reduce this overhead, yet existing methods often trail CoT and remain limited by single-path supervision and reasoning budgets that do not adapt to problem difficulty. We introduce AURAL, which models a distribution over multiple plausible reasoning continuations in latent space and jointly predicts chunks of future states to reduce sequential forward passes and reasoning latency. To provide initial supervision for latent reasoning, we construct AuralReason-683K: 683K bilingual speech utterances (about 1,000 hours) with concise CoT for emotion recognition, empathetic dialogue, and general reasoning. AURAL-RL then explores beyond these traces, rewarding concise reasoning that yields high-quality answers and adapting reasoning effort to each problem. Across two backbones, AURAL-RL achieves performance comparable to CoT-RL, with larger gains over the respective supervised checkpoints on most metrics. Analysis further shows that harder questions elicit more latent reasoning steps. On Qwen2.5-Omni, it reduces time to the first answer token by 11.8x, from 1.22 to 0.10 s, versus 0.05 s for direct answering.

authors: Songtao Li,Yijia Zhang,Jianyuan Yuan,Shidi Zhang,Fengyu Zhang,Hongfei Lin
title: Enhancing Biomedical Named Entity Recognition via Multiple Programming Languages Instruction Tuning and Ensemble Method
abstract: Instruction tuning has become a common paradigm for applying large language models (LLMs) to biomedical named entity recognition (BioNER). However, existing instruction-tuning approaches still face two key challenges. First, conventional natural-language instructions typically serialize BioNER annotations as flat textual outputs, providing limited structural constraints for typed entity extraction. Second, high-quality biomedical annotations are limited, and learning from a single serialized output form may restrict structural diversity and reduce model robustness. Although external biomedical knowledge can be introduced to alleviate data scarcity, it often requires costly resource construction. To address these challenges, we propose MITE, a Multiple Programming Languages Instruction Tuning and Ensemble method for BioNER. MITE reformulates BioNER as a structure-to-structure generation task by representing both instructions and entity outputs in code-formatted representations. Specifically, each training instance is transformed into multiple programming-language formats, including Python, C++, and Java, while preserving the same underlying entity semantics. These language-specific representations provide structurally diverse supervision without requiring external biomedical knowledge or additional annotations. During inference, MITE aggregates predictions from different code formats through an entity-level voting strategy, reducing language-specific prediction variance and improving robustness. Experiments on three widely used BioNER datasets demonstrate that MITE achieves competitive performance against representative BERT-based and LLM-based baselines, attaining the best results on two benchmarks. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of multi-language representations.

authors: Jiaqi Xue,Yanjun Wang,Xiangci Li,Lingbo Mo,Aritra Sengupta,Shweta Garg,Murali Krishna Ramanathan,Myeongsoo Kim
title: AECP: Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol for Multi-Agent Code Generation
abstract: As AI agents increasingly tackle complex repository-level coding tasks, distributing work across multiple agents is a natural way to scale beyond the capabilities of a single agent. To coordinate their interdependent work, these agents share findings and agree on interfaces between modules. However, exchanged information often serves only as context, leaving individual agents to interpret it and incorporate it into subsequent work. Consequently, shared findings may go unused and deviations from interface agreements may go undetected, undermining the reliability and efficiency of collaboration. This motivates moving part of the coordination responsibility from individual agents to the execution harness. To make shared information actionable during execution, we introduce the Artifact-Exclusive Communication Protocol (AECP). AECP requires agents to communicate exclusively through structured artifacts and specifies how the harness processes them. The harness supplies findings when agents access relevant code, screens implementations for mismatches with recorded interface commitments, and requires affected agents to revisit revised agreements. These coordination steps become part of harness execution rather than actions that agents must initiate from prior messages. Across Doc2Repo, NL2Repo, and CodeProjectEval, using closed- and open-source models including Opus-4.8 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, AECP improves average test pass rate by 28.2% and reduces average wall time by 16.5% relative to an agent team using free-form inter-agent messages. Artifact-exclusive communication also blocks the relay of malicious instructions between agents, reducing how often they reach other agents from 95% to 0% and how often those agents act on them from 40% to 0%.

authors: Shaokun Zhang,Yifan Zhang,Jian Hu,Yueying Li,Hao Zhang,Binfeng Xu,Jan Kautz,Yi Dong
title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
abstract: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the \href{this https URL}{Molt library}.

authors: Yaohui Zhang,Binxu Li,Haoyi Duan,Jiacheng Miao,Yixin Wang,Xinran Du,Chenyue Li,Shilong Liu,Kevin Wu,James Zou
title: PlotGround: Grounding Plot Digitization in Real Scientific Figures and Their Source Data
abstract: Scientific figures often encode quantitative results that are not readily available in machine-readable form, making accurate plot digitization important for verifying and reusing published findings. Yet it remains unclear how accurately current models recover plotted values from real scientific figures, as existing benchmarks rely largely on synthetic charts or cover only a limited range of chart types. We introduce PlotGround, an automated pipeline for building plot digitization benchmarks from real scientific figures and their author-released source data. PlotGround maps figures to source tables, identifies reconstructable panels, and generates quantitative questions with source-grounded reference values. We use PlotGround to construct PlotGround-1k, a human-verified benchmark of 1,119 questions from 1,066 bioRxiv preprints. Across sixteen multimodal models, the best reaches 87.5% accuracy at a $\pm 5\%$ relative-error tolerance. Tightening the tolerance to $\pm 2\%$ lowers every model's accuracy by 11-24 percentage points, revealing a gap between approximate visual reading and precise quantitative recovery. PlotGround's paired figure-source structure lets us compare how accurately the same values are recovered from figures and from source tables. Providing source tables instead of figures raises a coding agent's accuracy from 90.0% to 97.4% while cutting cost by 72%.

authors: M. Yigit Turali,Shreyas Rajesh,M. Efe Lorasdagi,Chenda Duan,Kartik Sharma,Vwani Roychowdhury
title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

authors: Yuchen Li,Xintong Li,Zongqi Fan,Ken-tye Yong,Nguyen H. Tran
title: Where Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model? -- From Self-Index to Self-Reference
abstract: We separate two functional levels of self familiar from biology: a self-index, which separates one's own from external material and shapes processing, as corollary discharge does in nearly all animals, and self-reference, the higher ability to recognize what is one's own, as in mirror self-recognition. We probe both by placing the same text in an Assistant, User, or System message rendered by the model's own chat template. In Qwen3.8-27B we report three levels of evidence. Persistence: as predicted in advance, the representation of the text separates the model's own message from both external sources at all 64 layers and for every text. Coupling: asked who wrote the preceding message, the model claims its own messages (0.77) and assigns User and System messages alike to the user, and how strongly it claims each message is predicted by the size of its self-index (Spearman up to 0.68). Intervention: exchanging the internal states that follow a message reverses the self-attribution between layers 15 and 31; removing the self-index direction from them at layer 39 lowers the claim more than a random direction; and in arithmetic the model adopts a wrong step more often when it wrote the step itself (0.92 versus 0.75). Across eight open-weight models from four families, the levels are nested and do not follow model size: three models show neither, three a self-index without self-reference, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next recognizes its own messages only after reasoning (0.66, none of the external ones), and only Qwen3.8-27B shows both without thinking; no model shows self-reference without a self-index, and reasoning brings it out only where one exists. We propose that self-reference is a higher-level ability built on a self-index, a content-independent displacement superimposed on the whole representation of the model's own messages, and that neither level is a by-product of problem-solving ability.

authors: Stylianos Psychias,Yingqiang Gao
title: AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences
abstract: Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.

authors: Stylianos Psychias
title: UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison
abstract: Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification. This paper describes our participation in all three subtasks (ST1 binary fallacy detection, ST2 eight-way fallacy classification, ST3 four-way argument-scheme classification) and both evaluation tracks. Our submitted systems are fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small batch of LLM-generated synthetic contrastive pairs; for ST2 and ST3 on the enhanced track we additionally added confidence-filtered pseudo-labelled examples from the unlabelled pool. A wider backbone comparison spanning additional encoders (DeBERTa-v3, ModernBERT) and an LLM track (four Qwen variants from 3B to 32B, zero-shot through CoT-LoRA) showed no validated benefit over RoBERTa-large at this corpus scale, with 5-fold variance wide enough that we call the comparison underpowered rather than settled. We also characterise how much of the enhanced track's lift reflects organiser-rewritten inputs carrying label information rather than genuine argument clarification. On the official Touche 2026 test set our systems ranked first on both base-track classification cells (ST2 and ST3) and second on both binary-detection (ST1) tracks, with the two enhanced-track classification cells topped by cascaded and multitask systems. We close with the rare-class limitation on ST3 and the most useful follow-ups. Code:this https URL

authors: Husein Zolkepli
title: Where Words Begin and End
abstract: Forced aligners locate each word of a known transcript in the audio, and many speech pipelines depend on them. In our own data, a widely used CTC aligner inserts a pause at nearly every word boundary, and we found almost no aligner evaluated on telephone audio. We compare nine aligner configurations against human word boundaries on read, conversational and telephone English. The Montreal Forced Aligner (MFA) is the most precise, while CTC aligners consistently start words late, because most frames inside a word go to the blank token. We then fine-tune Whisper with LoRA to predict each word's start and end as timestamp tokens, training only on boundaries placed by people: 47 hours in 87 languages. The resulting aligner is more precise than MFA on every English test condition, and than MFA's own Korean and Dutch models. With FA-Bench's protocol and code on TIMIT, its word-boundary error is 11.6 ms, against 18.2 ms for the best published system. Two choices matter most on telephone conversations: placing the timestamp slots after the word they time, and training on noisy transcripts, which also makes the aligner nearly insensitive to errors in the transcript. The released model reaches 16.0 ms on real landline calls, against 36.5 ms for MFA. The models are available atthis https URL

authors: Soovadeep Bakshi,Apurba Bose,Aishwarya Bose,Sandip Nandi
title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

authors: Mingyu Lu,Timothy Ossowski,Tristan Naumann,Hoifung Poon,Peniel Argaw
title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
abstract: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce HERO Harnessing Evidence for Refinement and Optimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, HERO learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, HERO achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by 7.6 points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another 2.0 points and improves execution efficiency.

authors: Yiheng Su,Junyi Jessy Li,Matthew Lease
title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. DualView first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

authors: Oscar Chew,Po-Yi Lu,Yi-Jie Cheng,Kunal Jain,Hsuan-Tien Lin,Zhengzhong Tu,Kuan-Hao Huang
title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

authors: Xiaohan Wang,Haozhen Zhang,Qingyuan Liu,Tao Feng,Wenya Wang
title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

authors: Bohan Sun,Zunhai Su,Xialie Zhuang,Jianjin Li,Ngai Wong,Chuan-Wei Kuo
title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Alessandro Rozza,Davide Mambelli,Steven Motta,Juri Taresch
title: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models
abstract: An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.

authors: Yufan Zhu,Yangfan Jiang,Yang Fei,Shizheng Hou,Shubhankar Mohapatra,Xiaokui Xiao
title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery
abstract: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.

authors: Sergio Burdisso,Esaú Villatoro-Tello,Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés,Yanis Labrak,Jordi Luque,Milos Cernak,Petr Motlicek
title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under open licenses atthis https URL, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

authors: Jian Gu,Hongyu Zhang,Chunyang Chen,Aldeida Aleti
title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics
abstract: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics, and the embedding and unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods reuse a fixed lens or treat states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state as the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that remain and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it in a model-native and context-aware way, reading a state through the remaining layers with a given number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, fitting nothing to the model's output. No lens with fixed directions per layer can reach a mean cosine with the native frame's lexical readouts above the square root of their coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B. LexFrame[1], of order 1, reaches 0.97 and 0.97, and its readings are on average within 0.16 and 0.15 nats of the model's output. Its coefficient differences attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, and its lexical basis steers predictions while sparing other tokens. On average, its readings settle on the model's top token over the final 0.82 and 0.81 of the layers, those of lenses over at most 0.11. These frames thus make every hidden state readable, attributable and steerable.

authors: Emmanouil Zaranis,António Farinhas,Saul Santos,Beatriz Canaverde,Miguel Moura Ramos,Aditya K Surikuchi,André Viveiros,Baohao Liao,Elena Bueno-Benito,Nithin Sivakumaran,Pavlo Vasylenko,Shoubin Yu,Sonal Sannigrahi,Wafaa Mohammed,Ben Peters,Danae Sánchez Villegas,Elias Stengel-Eskin,Giuseppe Attanasio,Jaehong Yoon,Stella Frank,Alessandro Suglia,Chrysoula Zerva,Desmond Elliott,Mariella Dimiccoli,Mohit Bansal,Oswald Lanz,Raffaella Bernardi,Raquel Fernández,Sandro Pezzelle,Vlad Niculae,André F. T. Martins
title: How Well Do Vision-Language Models Understand Movies?
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can increasingly handle extended contexts and answer questions about long videos--but can they understand the narrative structure of movies as humans do? To investigate this question, we introduce MF$^2$ (Movie Facts and Fibs), a fully manually curated benchmark designed to evaluate whether models can identify, recall, and comprehend information central to the movie's storyline, using both the visual and textual modalities. MF$^2$ includes over 50 open-licensed movies, each paired with manually constructed sets of claim pairs: one true claim (fact) and one plausible but false (fib), totaling over 850 pairs. Our analysis across 20 open-source and 2 proprietary models reveals a substantial gap relative to human performance. While subtitles provide a strong signal for narrative understanding, other textual sources (e.g., synopses) are less informative. In contrast, when visual information is distributed across the entire movie and jointly embedded with subtitles, models struggle to identify and effectively use the relevant content. However, when the visual input is restricted to claim-relevant visual content, models improve significantly, indicating substantial room for improvement in processing large multimodal contexts and distinguishing relevant from irrelevant information. Overall, our findings highlight persistent challenges in multimodal narrative understanding for current VLMs. We release our data and code to support further research in this direction.

authors: Sangwoo Park,Jinheon Baek,Soyeong Jeong,Sung Ju Hwang
title: Chain of Retrieval: Multi-Aspect Iterative Search Expansion and Post-Order Search Aggregation for Full Paper Retrieval
abstract: Scientific paper retrieval, particularly framed as document-to-document retrieval, aims to identify relevant papers in response to a long-form query paper, rather than a short query string. Previous approaches to this task have largely focused on abstracts, embedding them into dense vectors as surrogates for full documents and calculating similarity between them. Yet, abstracts offer only sparse and high-level summaries, and such methods primarily optimize one-to-one similarity, overlooking the dynamic relations that emerge across relevant papers during the retrieval process. To address this, we propose Chain of Retrieval (CoR), a novel iterative framework for full-paper retrieval. Specifically, CoR decomposes each query paper into multiple aspect-specific views, matches them against segmented candidate papers, and iteratively expands the search by promoting top-ranked results as new queries, thereby forming a tree-structured retrieval process. The resulting retrieval tree is then aggregated in a post-order manner: descendants are first combined at the query level, then recursively merged with their parent nodes, to capture hierarchical relations across iterations. To validate this, we present SciFullBench, a large-scale benchmark providing both complete and segmented contexts of full papers for queries and candidates, and results show that CoR significantly outperforms existing retrieval baselines. Our code and dataset is available atthis https URL.

authors: Shomir Wilson
title: NLP Meets the World: Toward Improving Conversations With News Media About Natural Language Processing Research
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have rapidly increased the public's interest in natural language processing (NLP). This attention is reflected by news outlets inviting NLP researchers to share their knowledge and views with public audiences. Recognizing the opportunities for the research field and for individual researchers, this paper shares recommendations for speaking with news media about NLP's capabilities and limitations. Drawing on the topical structure of research communication frameworks published by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine and the European Union's QUEST project, recommendations are provided for three field-appropriate communication challenges: cognitive terminology, unsustainable expectations, and ethical failures. Published NLP research and popular news coverage are cited to provide examples. The recommendations promote effective, transparent communication with the general public about NLP, in order to strengthen public understanding and encourage support for research.

authors: Pengcheng Huang,Tianming Liu,Zhenghao Liu,Yukun Yan,Shuo Wang,Tong Xiao,Zulong Chen,Maosong Sun
title: Empirical Analysis of Decoding Biases in Masked Diffusion Models
abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have recently emerged as a promising non-autoregressive paradigm for sequence generation. However, their performance is highly sensitive to the choice of decoding strategy. In this work, we reveal that prevalent uncertainty-based decoding strategies induce two decoding biases in MDMs: rigid boundary bias and trivial token bias. These biases limit the model's reasoning ability and ultimately degrade generation quality. To address these challenges, we propose UNmasking Calibration for DecOding DEbiasing (Uncode), a decoding calibration framework that regularizes uncertainty-based decoding by incorporating two complementary priors to shape global decoding trajectories and promote content informativeness. Extensive experiments on three advanced MDMs across seven reasoning- and planning-intensive benchmarks demonstrate that Uncode consistently outperforms existing decoding strategies by more than 7%, while achieving performance comparable to autoregressive models of similar parameter scales. The code is publicly available atthis https URL.

authors: NRIPESH NIKETAN,VAATSALYA SHRIVASTVA,BHUSHAN SRIVASTAVA,SUSHANT MISHRA
title: CrossTL: Hub-Based Translation of GPU Programs and the Preservation of Source Rules
abstract: GPU programs are written in vendor languages that disagree about integer overflow, division by zero, NaN handling, floating-point contraction, data layout and dispatch, so a translated program can compile and still compute something else. We describe CrossTL, an open-source translator that routes ten GPU source languages to eleven targets through CrossGL, a textual hub language, with repository-scale porting, contracts that loaders check, and native parity tests. We define faithful translation as refinement up to rejection under a compile configuration, and test whether a hub that records each source rule and lowers it through one per-target table keeps rules that a syntax-only hub loses. On an internally pre-registered suite of 66 hazard kernels in six languages, run on an Apple GPU through Metal, MoltenVK and WebGPU and on CPU implementations of Vulkan, OpenGL and an emulated Direct3D 12, SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with Metal's math mode and between two Vulkan implementations. A rule-carrying prototype of the hub removes 34 of 39 divergences on the rules it carries, against 14 for local fixes to four SPIR-V defects, and refuses where WGSL cannot express a rule. The registered hypothesis that it keeps every rule fails: MoltenVK, a non-conformant Vulkan layer, drops a rule that correct SPIR-V carries natively. On 2,585 programs written by third parties, 31% of CrossTL's translations are usable, established translators produce valid output significantly more often in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes no target's accepted share by more than 0.2 points. Recording each operation's source rule suffices for the rules tested but is not necessary: one strongest rule would keep them too, at about nine times as many rewrites and 58 more refusals on the corpus.

authors: Deepak Bastola,Woohyeok Choi
title: Hybrid Topic-Semantic Labeling and Graph Embeddings for Unsupervised Legal Document Clustering
abstract: Legal documents pose substantial challenges for unsupervised knowledge discovery due to specialized domain terminology, multi-scale document lengths, and scarce expert annotations. This paper introduces Topic-Graph Spherical Fusion (TGSF), a dual-manifold representation learning framework for unsupervised legal document clustering that unifies dense topic-semantic discovery and relational graph embeddings on a joint unit hypersphere. Instantiating dense topic discovery via Top2Vec and biased second-order random walks via Node2Vec, TGSF constructs a connected multi-relational document-topic graph combining multi-topic centroid bridges with temperature-sharpened semantic k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) document edges, guaranteeing a single connected component. The resulting L2-normalized semantic and graph representations are fused via modality-weighted concatenation onto a joint unit hypersphere prior to KMeans partitioning, decomposing squared chordal distance into a convex combination of semantic and structural cosine similarities. Evaluations across three legal benchmarks (ACORD, CUAD, and LEDGAR) show that TGSF outperforms semantic-only, structural-only, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TF-IDF baselines. Across 216 factorial grid configurations and 240 Bayesian TPE and Multi-Objective NSGA-II Pareto optimization trials per dataset (720 trials total), TGSF improves Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) from 0.606 to 0.653 on LEDGAR (ARI = 0.425), 0.228 to 0.284 on ACORD (ARI = 0.260), and 0.535 to 0.570 on CUAD (ARI = 0.282). Functional ANOVA and Pareto frontier diagnostics further characterize hyperparameter sensitivity for reproducible legal text mining.

authors: Marianna Nezhurina,Harsh Raj,Victor May,Jörg Franke,Taishi Nakamura,Timur Carstensen,Niccolò Ajroldi,Ville Komulainen,David Salinas,Jenia Jitsev
title: Open-sci-ref-0.02: open reference baselines for reproducible language model and dataset comparison
abstract: Reliable progress in language modeling depends on knowing whether a new dataset, architecture, or training recipe is genuinely better than existing alternatives. To foster reproducible learning procedure comparison, we present open-sci-ref, a family of dense transformers trained as open reference baselines at four scales (0.13B-1.7B parameters) on nine main reference datasets, with token budgets up to 1T, using a single tuned and fully documented training procedure. To facilitate a shared experimentation and measurement infrastructure, we release model weights, intermediate checkpoints, training logs, code, and downstream evaluations. When comparing training procedures, we take into account total compute spent. Placing training procedures on a common compute axis helps identify reference points that are weak or strong for the compute they use, without requiring a full scaling law study for every comparison. We identify Nemotron-CC-HQ as the strongest reference dataset on our evaluation suite: our 1.7B model trained on 1T of its tokens matches SmolLM2-1.7B with roughly 11$\times$ less compute. Shared baselines expose pitfalls of scaling trend comparisons: when a small-scale point is unusually weak, the resulting slope can overstate the scalability of a training procedure. We illustrate this diagnostically with EuroLLM-1.7B, which underperforms 300B token FineWeb-Edu baseline despite 13$\times$ more training compute. As an additional case study, the suite supports controlled comparison between permissively licensed and mixed-license datasets: the permissive-first MixtureVitae dataset changes rank substantially with scale. This also illustrates why data ranking should be evaluated through multi-scale reference trajectories rather than single proxy runs. All artifacts are publicly released.

authors: Tobias Holtdirk,Dennis Assenmacher,Arnim Bleier,Claudia Wagner
title: Learning from Convenience Samples: Fine-Tuning LLMs to Predict Voting Choices from Biased Survey Samples
abstract: Survey research increasingly relies on convenience samples as rising costs and nonresponse make representative probability sampling more difficult. This creates a central challenge for public opinion research and electoral studies: how to recover reliable population-level inferences from socially and demographically biased data. While recent work has explored the use of large language models (LLMs) for simulating survey responses, most studies focus on the U.S. population and assume relatively favourable data conditions with limited or random missingness. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can leverage contextual knowledge about socio-demographic and political patterns to predict vote choice in the German population under sampling constraints. We systematically vary both the size and composition of training data, ranging from large representative samples to small, biased convenience samples, and compare zero-shot prompting and supervised fine-tuning against established tabular classifiers such as CatBoost.Our results show that when representative training data are available, fine-tuned LLMs achieve predictive performance comparable to strong tabular baselines and substantially outperform zero-shot prompting. Under small and biased convenience samples, however, fine-tuned LLMs more accurately recover both individual-level vote choice and population-level distributions than zero-shot approaches and often outperform tabular methods. These findings suggest that fine-tuned LLMs can combine sample-specific information with contextual knowledge acquired during pre-training, enabling more robust inference under conditions of sampling bias and missing data.

authors: Claas Beger,Ryan Yi,Shuhao Fu,Kaleda Denton,Arseny Moskvichev,Sarah W. Tsai,Sivasankaran Rajamanickam,Melanie Mitchell
title: Distinguishing Performance From Competence in Evaluations of Humanlike Abstract Reasoning
abstract: AI reasoning models have exceeded human performance on the ARC-AGI-1 benchmark, but does that mean state-of-the-art models have the underlying competence (humanlike abstract reasoning) that the benchmark was designed to test? Here we investigate the abstraction abilities of AI models using the closely related but simpler ConceptARC benchmark. Our evaluations vary input modality (textual vs. visual), use of external Python tools, and reasoning effort. Beyond output accuracy, we evaluate the natural-language rules that models generate to explain their solutions, enabling us to assess whether models recognize the abstractions that ConceptARC was designed to elicit. We show that the best models' rules are frequently based on less abstract, more domain-specific concepts, capturing intended abstractions considerably less often than humans. In the visual modality, AI models' output accuracy drops sharply; however, our rule-level analysis reveals that a substantial share of their rules capture intended abstractions, even as the models struggle to apply these concepts to generate correct solutions. In short, we show that using performance (accuracy) alone can substantially overestimate AI competence in textual modalities while underestimating it in visual modalities, an illustration of the risk of mistaking performance for competence.

authors: Chengyi Yang,Zhishang Xiang,Yunbo Tang,Zongpei Teng,Chengsong Huang,Fei Long,Yuhan Liu,Jinsong Su
title: TTCS: Test-Time Curriculum Synthesis for Self-Evolving
abstract: Test-Time Training offers a promising way to improve the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) by adapting the model using only the test questions. However, existing methods struggle with difficult reasoning problems for two reasons: raw test questions are often too difficult to yield high-quality pseudo-labels, and the limited size of test sets makes continuous online updates prone to instability. To address these limitations, we propose TTCS, a co-evolving test-time training framework. Specifically, TTCS initializes two policies from the same pretrained model: a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver. These policies evolve through iterative optimization: the synthesizer generates progressively challenging question variants conditioned on the test questions, creating a structured curriculum tailored to the solver's current capability, while the solver updates itself using self-consistency rewards computed from multiple sampled responses on both original test and synthetic questions. Crucially, the solver's feedback guides the synthesizer to generate questions aligned with the model's current capability, and the generated question variants in turn stabilize the solver's test-time training. Experiments show that TTCS consistently strengthens the reasoning ability on challenging mathematical benchmarks and transfers to general-domain tasks across different LLM backbones, highlighting a scalable path towards dynamically constructing test-time curricula for self-evolving. Our code and implementation details are available atthis https URL.

authors: Tim Schlippe,Simon Martin,Michael Marketsmüller
title: RAG Strategies for Natural Language-Based SQL Query and REST API Call Generation
abstract: Enterprise software systems commonly expose functionality through relational databases and REST APIs, requiring users to understand schemas, endpoints, and parameters. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can support natural language interfaces by grounding large language models (LLMs) in enterprise-specific documentation. We evaluate three training-free RAG configurations - Standard RAG, Relevance Filtering RAG, and Iterative Retrieval RAG - for SQL query generation, REST API call generation, and a combined task requiring routing between both operation types. Using SAP Transactional Banking, we constructed an expert-reviewed dataset with mock execution screening and compared the configurations under database-only, API-only, and mixed-documentation settings. Without retrieval, exact match accuracy is 0% across all tasks, whereas retrieval achieves mock execution success of up to 79.30% and component match accuracy of up to 78.86%. In the combined task, Iterative Retrieval RAG achieves higher exact match accuracy than Standard RAG (10.29% vs. 7.45%), with similar mock execution success (68.93% vs. 67.10%). However, for REST API call generation under mixed documentation, Iterative Retrieval RAG achieves lower mock execution success than Standard RAG (50.53% vs. 75.79%). Overall, retrieval-control strategies show task- and metric-dependent behavior under mixed-documentation settings.

authors: Jiwoo Hong,Shao Tang,Zhipeng Wang
title: Bayesian Preference Learning for Test-Time Steerable Reward Models
abstract: Reward models are central to aligning language models with human preferences via reinforcement learning (RL). As RL is increasingly applied to settings such as verifiable rewards and multi-objective alignment, RMs are expected to encode more complex and multifaceted preference distributions. However, classifier RMs remain static once trained, limiting their adaptability at test time. We propose Variational In-Context Reward Modeling (ICRM), a novel Bayesian reward modeling objective that enables test-time steerability via in-context preference demonstrations. ICRM casts reward modeling as amortized variational inference over a latent preference probability under the Bradley-Terry model using a conjugate Beta prior. We show that ICRM adapts to unseen preference distributions at test time for both single and multi-objective settings. With more demonstrations, ICRM improves RM-Bench accuracy from 60.5 to 70.8, achieves lower calibration error than a generative judge on moral dilemma preferences, and expands the attainable Pareto frontier under conflicting preferences. We further study the practical applicability of ICRM for RL training, showing that it can effectively encode verifiable rewards by outperforming a conventional RM in math reasoning. Finally, we provide theoretical guarantees that the variational objective admits a global interior optimum with finite confidence, followed by an ablation study on its role for the test-time steerability, and we analyze how KL regularization mitigates reward over-optimization.

authors: Xiaohan Zhao,Zhaoyi Li,Yaxin Luo,Jiacheng Cui,Zhiqiang Shen
title: Pushing the Frontier of Black-Box LVLM Attacks via Fine-Grained Detail Targeting
abstract: Black-box adversarial attacks on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are challenging due to missing gradients and complex multimodal boundaries. Prior state-of-the-art transfer-based approaches such as M-Attack match local crops between source and target images, but this induces high-variance, nearly orthogonal gradients across iterations. We attribute this instability to (i) ViT translation sensitivity, which yields spike-like gradients, and (ii) a structural asymmetry between source and target crops. We reformulate local matching as an asymmetric expectation over source transformations and target semantics, and introduce M-Attack-V2 based on this formulation. Multi-Crop Alignment (MCA) averages gradients from multiple local views per iteration, while Auxiliary Target Alignment (ATA) replaces aggressive target augmentation with a small set of semantically correlated auxiliary images. Patch Momentum replays historical crop gradients, and a patch-diverse surrogate ensemble (PE+) strengthens transferable directions. M-Attack-V2 raises attack success rates over M-Attack from 40% to 61% on GPT-6.1 Sol, from 40% to 60% on GPT-6 Astra, and from 85% to 97% on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Code and data are publicly available at:this https URL.

authors: Kyle Janse van Rensburg,Benjamin van Niekerk,Herman Kamper
title: Interpreting Speaker Characteristics in the Dimensions of Self-Supervised Speech Features
abstract: How do speech models trained through self-supervised learning structure their representations? Previous studies have looked at how information is encoded in feature vectors across different layers. But few studies have considered whether speech characteristics are captured \textit{within} individual dimensions of SSL features. In this paper, we specifically look at speaker information using PCA on utterance-averaged representations. For a range of SSL models, we find that the principal dimension that explains most variance encodes pitch and associated characteristics like gender. Other individual principal dimensions correlate with intensity, noise levels, the second formant, and higher frequency characteristics. We then use synthesis analyses to show that the dimensions for most characteristics are isolated from each other's influence. We further show that characteristics can be changed by manipulating the corresponding dimensions.

authors: Yu Wu,Guangzeng Han,Ibra Niang Niang,Francia Ravelombola,Maiara Oliveira,Jason Davis,Dong Chen,Feng Lin,Xiaolei Huang
title: From Scientific Crop Imagery to Agronomic Reasoning: A Multimodal LLM Benchmark for Plant Phenotyping
abstract: High-throughput, effective and comprehensive phenotyping is a critical prerequisite for crop improvement. While phenotypic analysis was traditionally performed manually, recent advances in multimodal foundation models, especially in vision-language models, have offered new opportunities for automated plant phenotyping. However, plant science remains particularly challenging for general-purpose VLMs because it requires domain-specific knowledge, fine-grained visual interpretation, and complex agronomic reasoning. We introduce PlantXpert, an evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning benchmark for plant phenotyping across four major crops: soybean, cotton, rice, and corn. Our benchmark provides a structured and reproducible framework for agronomic adaptation of VLMs, and enables controlled comparison between base models and their domain-adapted counterparts. We constructed a dataset comprising 545 digital images and 4,351 benchmark samples spanning key agronomic domains including disease, pest control, weed management and yield. The benchmark can assess diverse capabilities including visual expertise, quantitative reasoning, and multi-step agronomic reasoning. We trained and evaluated a total of 11 state-of-the-art VLMs. Fine-tuning on our dataset improves overall accuracy for all models, with many achieving around 70% accuracy, and improvements on 9 of 11 remaining statistically significant after Holm correction. We also identify diminishing returns from model scaling, uneven performance across crop subsets, and persistent weaknesses in quantitative reasoning and specialized image analysis. These limitations show that general multimodal competence alone is insufficient for reliable agronomic reasoning and demonstrate the value of domain-specific adaptation. We hope PlantXpert can serve as a foundation for advancing evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in plant science.

authors: Chenming Tang,Hsiu-Yuan Huang,Weijie Liu,Junqiang Zheng,Saiyong Yang,Yunfang Wu
title: Democratizing Tool Learning with Environments Fully Simulated by a Free 8B Language Model
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a prevalent paradigm for training tool calling agents, which typically requires online interactive environments. Existing approaches either rely on training data with ground truth annotations or require advanced proprietary language models (LMs) to synthesize environments that remain fixed once created. In this work, we propose TRUSTEE, a cost-friendly method for training tool calling agents with dynamic environments fully simulated by open-source LMs that can be as small as 8B, including task generation, user simulation, tool simulation, and trajectory evaluation, paired with an adaptive curriculum learning mechanism that controls task difficulty dynamically. Our empirical results show that TRUSTEE outperforms baselines which require extra external resources in most cases. These confirm that, with a sufficiently sophisticated design, even simulated environments with a local 8B LM as the backbone could set a strong baseline for tool learning. We hope our proposed paradigm could democratize tool learning and inspire future research on environment scaling with limited resources.

authors: Namyoung So,Seokgyu Jang,Taeuk Kim
title: Superficial Success vs. Internal Breakdown: An Empirical Study of Generalization in Adaptive Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Adaptive multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly adopted to tackle complex problems. However, the narrow task coverage of their optimization raises the question of whether they can function as general-purpose systems. To address this gap, we conduct an extensive empirical study of adaptive MAS, revealing two key findings: (1) topological overfitting -- they fail to generalize across different domains; and (2) illusory coordination -- they achieve reasonable surface-level accuracy while the underlying agent interactions diverge from ideal MAS behavior, raising concerns about their practical utility. These findings highlight the pressing need to prioritize generalization in MAS development and motivate evaluation protocols that extend beyond simple final-answer correctness. We release our code at this https URL.

authors: Shakeel Sheikh,Patrick Marmaroli,MD Sahidullah,Slim Ouni,Fabrice Hirsch,Goncalo Leal,Bjorn W Schuller
title: Virtual Speech Therapist: A Clinician-in-the-Loop AI Agent for Speech Therapy Planning
abstract: This paper presents a proof of concept of the Virtual Speech Therapist (VST), an intelligent multi-agent based system designed to support stuttering assessment and individualized therapy planning through artificial intelligence (AI) driven workflows. VST integrates deep learning (DL) based stuttering detection fSD with large language model (LLM) based agentic system to assist clinicians in developing evidence informed therapy plans. The VST system begins with the acquisition and feature extraction of given speech samples, followed by the detection of stuttering types. Building on these speech driven information S, VST initiates an agentic reasoning process in which specialized LLM agents autonomously generate, critique, and iteratively refine individualized therapy plans P. A dedicated CriticAgent {\pi}ca acts as a structured self-refinement mechanism, reviewing the generated therapy plans P and identifying areas for potential improvement in consistency, methodological soundness, and alignment with available evidence and professional guidelines. The resulting therapy plan P is presented then as a draft for clinician review. Clinician feedback can then be incorporated to produce a revised plan P, thereby maintaining a clinician-in-the-loop (CITL) paradigm. An initial evaluation, involving expert speech language pathologist (SLP) examines the clinical interpretability and feasibility of the generated therapy plans. Taken together, the results show the potential of VST to augment clinician-led therapy planning and provide a promising basis for future studies evaluating its integration into real world clinical settings. An interactive user interface for the proposed prototype is available online at:this https URL, facilitating interactive stuttering assessment and stuttering therapy planning.

authors: Polydoros Giannouris,Yuechen Jiang,Lingfei Qian,Yuyan Wang,Xueqing Peng,Jimin Huang,Guojun Xiong,Sophia Ananiadou
title: MOIRA: Policy Memory and Belief Revision for Language-Model Agents in Non-Stationary Pair Trading
abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems exhibit hierarchical structure, where high-level semantic choices constrain downstream actions and feedback is delayed and ambiguous. Learning in such settings is challenging due to credit assignment: performance degradation may arise from flawed abstractions, suboptimal execution, or their interaction. We study this challenge through pair trading, a domain that naturally combines long-horizon semantic reasoning for asset pair selection with short-horizon execution under partial observability. We formulate pair trading as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem and propose a language-driven optimization framework in which both high-level and low-level policies are parameterized by large language models (LLMs) and optimized exclusively through prompt updates. Our approach leverages pretrained LLMs as hierarchical policies and uses trajectory- and episode-level textual feedback to adapt abstractions and execution without gradient-based fine-tuning. By explicitly separating abstraction selection from execution, the framework reduces non-stationarity across hierarchical levels and enables targeted adaptation under delayed feedback. Experiments on real-world market data show consistent improvements over traditional and LLM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning.

authors: Ruiyang Qin,Qingzhuo Wang,Dongrui Liu,Qiang Li,Zhihua Wei,Wen Shen
title: Multilingual Safety Alignment via Self-Distillation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit severe multilingual safety misalignment: they possess strong safeguards in high-resource languages but remain highly vulnerable to jailbreak attacks in low-resource languages. Current safety alignment methods generally rely on high-quality response data for each target language, which is expensive and difficult to generate. In this paper, we propose a cross-lingual safeguard transfer framework named Multilingual Self-Distillation (MSD). This framework transfers an LLM's inherent safety capabilities from high-resource (e.g., English) to low-resource (e.g., Javanese) languages, overcoming the need for response data in any language. Our framework is flexible and can be integrated with different self-distillation strategies. Specifically, we implement two concrete methods -- on-policy MSD and off-policy MSD -- both of which enable effective cross-lingual safety transfer using only multilingual queries. Furthermore, we propose Dual-Perspective Safety Weighting (DPSW), a divergence measure to optimize the distillation objective. By jointly considering the perspectives of both the teacher and the student, DPSW adaptively increases the penalty weights on safety-critical tokens while reducing the weights on non-critical tokens. Extensive experiments on representative LLMs across diverse multilingual jailbreak and utility benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently achieves superior multilingual safety performance. Notably, it generalizes effectively to more challenging datasets and unseen languages while preserving the model's general capabilities.

authors: Yixuan Mei,Zikun Li,Zixuan Chen,Shiqi Pan,Mengdi Wu,Xupeng Miao,Zhihao Jia,K. V. Rashmi
title: Coral: Cost-Efficient Multi-LLM Serving over Heterogeneous Cloud GPUs
abstract: The landscape of large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly fragmented, with no single model dominating the field. Meanwhile, cloud providers offer a diverse array of mid-tier and older-generation GPUs. These heterogeneous resources provide better availability and deliver comparable performance-per-dollar to top-tier hardware. To efficiently harness these GPUs for concurrent multi-LLM serving, we introduce Coral: an adaptive, heterogeneity-aware serving system. The key idea behind Coral is the joint optimization of resource allocation and replica serving strategies across all models. To keep pace with shifting throughput demands and resource availability, Coral employs a lossless, two-stage decomposition. This approach preserves joint optimality while reducing online solve times from hours to mere tens of seconds. Evaluations across 6 models and 20 GPU configurations demonstrate that Coral reduces serving costs by up to 2.79$\times$ compared to the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 2.39$\times$ higher goodput under scarce resource constraints.

authors: Dan Ofer,Oriel Perets,Michal Linial,Nadav Rappoport
title: ProtSent: Protein Sentence Transformers
abstract: Protein language models produce rich per-residue representations, but the sequence embeddings obtained by mean-pooling them are never trained to place related proteins near one another, so the geometry that retrieval, clustering and nearest-neighbor transfer depend on is never optimized. We present ProtSent, a contrastive post-training framework that supervises a protein language model with three types of biological relation at once, Pfam family co-membership, AlphaFold DB structural clusters and STRING interactions, and with deep mutational scanning fitness ordering as an optional fourth. It needs no structure at training or inference, trains on corpora filtered at 40% sequence identity against the benchmark test sets they most resemble, and is applied to ESM-2 (35M and 150M parameters) and ESM-C (300M). Post-training makes structural family membership recoverable from the frozen embedding without a trained readout: on SCOPe-40, the adjusted Rand index of the 35M model rises from 0.054 (near chance) to 0.507, and family retrieval gains +0.185, +0.190 and +0.424 Recall@1 over the three frozen backbones, with paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero. On the CATH midnight-zone benchmark, homologous-superfamily accuracy rises from 40.7% to 56.7% at 35M and from 43.3% to 62.7% at 150M, more than the 12 points a CATH-supervised model gains over its own base. Against a maximally sensitive HMMER search, alignment keeps the best single hit at both ESM-2 scales, but the embedding leads at ranking depth (MAP 0.705 against 0.607 at 150M) and returns a ranking for every query, including those where alignment finds none. Under a trained linear probe, however, the same embeddings fall below the untuned backbone, as do structure-distilled embeddings against theirs, so the gain in neighborhood structure comes at a cost in linear-probe accuracy. Code and models:this https URL

authors: Liangqi Yuan,Wenzhi Fang,Shiqiang Wang,Christopher G. Brinton
title: PAAC: Privacy-Aware Agentic Device-Cloud Collaboration
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents face a structural tension: cloud agents provide strong reasoning but expose user data, while on-device agents preserve privacy at the cost of overall capability. Existing device-cloud designs treat this boundary as a compute split rather than a trust boundary suited to agentic workloads, and existing sanitizers force a choice between policy flexibility and the structural fidelity tool calls require. In this work, we develop PAAC, a privacy-aware agentic framework that aligns planner--executor decomposition with the device-cloud boundary so that role specialization itself becomes the privacy mechanism. The cloud agent reasons over typed placeholder tokens that preserve each sensitive value's reasoning role while discarding its content, while the on-device agent identifies sensitive spans and distills each step's execution outcome into compact key findings. Sanitization confines the on-device LLM to proposing which spans to mask, while a deterministic registry performs all substitution and reversal, keeping actions directly executable on device. On three agentic benchmarks under strict privacy settings, PAAC dominates the Pareto frontier of privacy and accuracy, improving average accuracy by 15-36\% and reducing average leakage by 2-6$\times$ over state-of-the-art device-cloud baselines, with the largest margins on privacy targets outside fixed entity taxonomies. We find consistent improvements on 17 additional benchmarks spanning 10 domains, including math, science, and finance.

authors: Zi Liang,Ronghua Li,Yanyun Wang,Qingqing Ye,Haibo Hu
title: Mobius Injection: From One-Shot Prompt Injection to Sustained Resource Exhaustion in AI Agent Infrastructure
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have emerged as key intermediaries, orchestrating complex interactions between human users and a wide range of digital services and LLM infrastructures. While prior research has extensively examined the security of LLMs and agents in isolation, the systemic risk of the agent acting as a disruptive "hub" within the user-agent-service chain remains largely overlooked. In this work, we expose a novel threat paradigm by introducing Mobius Injection, a sophisticated attack that weaponizes autonomous agents into zombie nodes to launch what we define as Agent-based and -Oriented DDoS (AbO-DDoS) attacks. Mobius Injection composes known indirect prompt injection and persistent agent components through a distinct structural mechanism named Semantic Closure, which induces sustained recursive execution of agent components through a single injection event. We demonstrate that this attack is lightweight for the adversary, can evade traditional volumetric DDoS monitors and input filters calibrated for low false-positive rates, and is highly configurable, allowing for surgical targeting of specific environments or model providers.
