To evaluate the real-world impact, we conduct extensive experiments across three representative claw-style agents and three mainstream coding agents, integrated with 12 frontier proprietary or open-weight LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Mobius Injection achieves substantial attack success across diverse tasks, driving single-node call amplification up to 51.0x. Under coordinated multi-node pressure, each infected node still drains about 123k--127k tokens on a shared five-GPU backend; benign request latency rises by abou 23x--24x, and coordinated infections eventually saturate shared capacity until benign traffic is effectively denied service.

authors: Harshita Chopra,Kshitish Ghate,Aylin Caliskan,Tadayoshi Kohno,Chirag Shah,Natasha Jaques
title: Beyond Cooperative Simulators: Generating Realistic User Personas for Robust Evaluation of LLM Agents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact with diverse users, including those who are unclear, impatient, or reluctant to share information. However, collecting real interaction data at scale remains expensive. The field has turned to LLM-based \emph{user simulators} as stand-ins, but these simulators inherit the behavior of their underlying models: cooperative and homogeneous. As a result, agents that appear strong in simulation often fail in real human interactions. To narrow this gap, we introduce Persona Policies (PPol), a plug-and-play control layer that induces realistic behavioral variation in user simulators while preserving original task goals. Rather than hand-crafting personas, we employ an evolutionary coding agent to discover persona generation programs optimized for human-likeness and behavioral coverage over real user conversations. The evolved program generates diverse, human-like personas for any task in the domain. Across 4 benchmarks--including $\tau^2$-bench Retail and Airline, ColBench, and WildChat--evolved PPol yield 28-72% absolute gains in fitness score over the baseline simulator. In blinded evaluations, annotators judged PPol users as 'human' 80.4% of the time, nearly 2x more than the baseline simulators. Training agents with PPol also improves real-world performance: our user study with live human-agent interactions showed that fine-tuning with our method boosted task success by +23% over default baselines. PPol thus offers a novel approach to strengthen simulator-based evaluation and training without changing underlying tasks.

authors: Xueqing Peng,Zhuohan Xie,Yupeng Cao,Haohang Li,Lingfei Qian,Yan Wang,Vincent Jim Zhang,Huan He,Xuguang Ai,Linhai Ma,Ruoyu Xiang,Yueru He,Yi Han,Shuyao Wang,Yuqing Guo,Mingyang Jiang,Yilun Zhao,Youzhong Dong,Xiaoyu Wang,Yankai Chen,Ye Yuan,Qiyuan Zhang,Fuyuan Lyu,Haolun Wu,Yonghan Yang,Zichen Zhao,Yuyang Dai,Fan Zhang,Rania Elbadry,Ayesha Gull,Muhammad Usman Safder,Nuo Chen,Fengbin Zhu,Tianshi Cai,Zimu Wang,Polydoros Giannouris,Yuechen Jiang,Zhiwei Liu,Mohsinul Kabir,Yuyan Wang,Yixiang Zheng,Yangyang Yu,Weijin Liu,Wenbo Cao,Anke Xu,Peng Lu,Jerry Huang,Mingquan Lin,Prayag Tiwari,Yijia Zhao,Víctor Gutiérrez-Basulto,Xiao-Yang Liu,Kaleb E Smith,Jiahuan Pei,Arman Cohan,Jimin Huang,Yuehua Tang,Alejandro Lopez-Lira,Xi Chen,Xue Liu,Junichi Tsujii,Jian-Yun Nie,Sophia Ananiadou
title: Herculean: An Agentic Benchmark for Financial Intelligence
abstract: As AI agents advance, the central question is no longer whether they can solve isolated financial tasks, but whether their capabilities generalize across complete professional workflows. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this question because they evaluate either static competencies or agents within a single interaction structure. We introduce Herculean, a benchmark of end-to-end agentic financial intelligence that crosses agent architecture, backbone model, and four structurally distinct workflows: Trading, Hedging, Market Insights, and Auditing. Each workflow is implemented as an MCP skill that preserves its native state, actions, constraints, and outcome criteria, allowing intact agent systems to be evaluated under matched external conditions. Across 30 architecture--backbone configurations, we find that agent capability is not globally ordered. Workflow rankings are weakly aligned, changing the architecture frequently reverses performance under the same backbone, and each architecture concentrates failure in different forms of workflow control. These results establish that agent performance is an interaction between architecture and workflow demand, rather than an intrinsic property of the underlying model. Consequently, success on a single financial workflow provides little evidence of dependable, general financial intelligence.

authors: Sarkar Snigdha Sarathi Das,Palash Goyal,Mihir Parmar,Nanyun Peng,Vishy Tirumalashetty,Chun-Liang Li,Rui Zhang,Jinsung Yoon,Tomas Pfister
title: Nexus : An Agentic Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Language models have emerged as highly capable reasoners, yet their performance in time series forecasting remains uneven across domains and levels of contextual grounding. This is primarily due to their suboptimal time series reasoning and numerical modeling capabilities. To tackle this, we introduce Nexus, a multimodal forecasting framework that bridges qualitative event reasoning with structural numerical modeling through principled statistical synthesis. Nexus follows three structured stages: (1) Temporal profiling and anchor generation, which distills the multimodal history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and generates a forecast anchor (2) Dual contextual outlook generation, which produces decoupled macro and micro level forecast trajectories, and (3) Bayesian synthesis, which reconciles the forecasting anchor with both contextual forecast trajectories via closed-form Gaussian updating weighted by empirical error covariances. Evaluated across three diverse forecasting benchmarks constituting eight datasets spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks, and purely numerical series, Nexus consistently outperforms leading time-series foundation models and language model baselines, while providing interpretable causal reasoning.

authors: Yihong Dong,Jiaru Qian,Haoran Zhang,Peixu Wang,Binhua Li,Zhi Jin,Yongbin Li,Ge Li,Xiaokang Yang,Xue Jiang
title: Agentic Reverse Engineering: From I/O to Code with Discovery Agent
abstract: The automatic synthesis of a program from any form of specification is regarded as a holy grail of computer science. Fueled by LLMs, NL2Code has achieved tremendous success, yet the fundamentally more challenging task of synthesizing programs from input-output behavior, which we refer to as IO2Code, remains largely unsolved. Whereas NL2Code can exploit the semantic alignment between natural language and code acquired during pretraining, IO2Code requires recovering underlying principles from concrete computational behavior, navigating a vast and underspecified hypothesis space. To address this, we propose DIO-Agent, a discovery agent that performs agentic reverse engineering from input-output behavior to code. Our method frames IO2Code as an evolutionary search over discrete program space, in which an LLM serves as the mutation operator and concrete error signals from execution guide each mutation. To prevent the search from wandering into structurally complex yet incorrect dead ends, we introduce the Transformation Priority Premise as a mutation prior that biases the LLM toward the simplest hypothesis consistent with current evidence, progressively escalating from constants to conditionals to iteration only when simpler constructs are insufficient. To facilitate systematic study, we further construct an IO2CodeBench spanning multiple difficulty levels. Extensive experiments show that DIO-Agent consistently outperforms both traditional program-by-example method and SOTA evolution-agent baselines across all difficulty levels and various LLMs, while substantially surpassing test-time scaling strategies with equivalent sampling budgets.

authors: Yuyang Zhang,Yifu Zhang,Xuehai Zhou,Xiaoyin Chen
title: A Measure-Theoretic Analysis of Reasoning in Transformers: Structural Generalization and Approximation Limits
abstract: Scaling laws for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) are well documented, but little theory explains their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. We formalize reasoning with optimal transport: each search trajectory is mapped to twelve structural coordinates, such as tree depth and backtracking rate, and dataset shift is measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance. Kantorovich duality bounds the OOD risk through this distance, the architecture's Lipschitz constant and approximation limits. First, under absolute positional encoding (APE), shifting part of a trajectory to later positions almost surely changes the attention scores within that part; if this misroutes exact-match search, the Lipschitz constant and risk are $\Omega(1)$. Shift-invariant encodings such as rotary position embedding (RoPE) leave the scores unchanged and bound the error. Second, we map backtracking to a Dyck-$k$ language and, under an implicit-depth assumption, derive a risk floor for search trees deeper than a multiple of the number of layers. Enough layers remove this floor; more width only shrinks a separate Barron-space approximation term. Experiments with 54 trained Transformers on combinatorial search (Countdown) support these bounds. Appendix experiments measure structural shifts in public agent, embodied and robot trajectories, shift all position indices of 33 public language models, and split deeply nested tasks into separate model calls.

authors: Lei Yang,Siyu Ding,Deyi Xiong
title: Local Conflict, Targeted Repair: A Perturbation Analysis of Multi-Domain RL
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves large language models on individual domains but can degrade previously acquired capabilities. We study this interference in mathematical reasoning, code generation, question answering (QA), and creative writing (CW). Full-model domain gradients can be nearly orthogonal despite substantial selective degradation. Our structural analyses show sparse, weakly overlapping edits on computation routes that reasoning domains share, with directional alignment associated with transfer and conflict. A local perturbation model separates loss changes into a first-order term and a path-averaged curvature term, decomposes the latter along the actual rollback intervention, and provides a conditional explanation for recovery by short refresh. The experiments support this local sensitivity account. After Code $\rightarrow$ Math $\rightarrow$ QA $\rightarrow$ CW training, a short Re-Math refresh raises Math from 57.66 to 66.04 and achieves the highest average score among the evaluated baselines. A training-free rollback at a $9.8\%$ budget recovers $57.4\%$ of the QA-induced Math accuracy drop with a small QA change. Curvature probes at the Math checkpoint further show higher sensitivity along the selected direction than along matched random directions. Together, these results support sparse intervention and targeted refresh as effective ways to mitigate cross-domain degradation.

authors: Vignesh Nagarajan
title: CANVAS: Captioning Art with Narrative Visual-Audio AI Systems
abstract: For a person who is blind or has low vision (BLV), a painting is usually represented by a few words of alt-text, if anything at all. That text rarely conveys the colour, texture, mood or arrangement that a sighted visitor takes in, and rich audio descriptions are too slow and costly to produce by hand for most collections. This study asks how far off-the-shelf generative AI can close that gap. We built CANVAS, a no-code Zapier workflow that sends an artwork image to a multimodal large language model, checks the returned description, narrates it with a fixed ElevenLabs voice and logs every run. With prompt, pipeline and voice held constant, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5 Mini and Claude 3.5 Haiku each described the same 50 artworks, and we compared the 150 narrated descriptions artwork by artwork. Gemini and GPT-5 Mini wrote text of similar Flesch Reading Ease (49.95 and 49.47); Claude's was harder to read (37.35, p < 0.001), largely because it used longer words. Lexical diversity did not differ. The findings show both promise and a clear design requirement. All 150 narrated descriptions cost US\$5.10, so a first draft of audio description for an entire collection is affordable even for small museums and educators. Yet while every description conveyed colour, only 16-18% used explicit layout terms such as left, right, foreground or background, and at most 10% signalled uncertainty. Spatial structure must therefore be requested explicitly and checked by people; accuracy and usefulness to BLV listeners remain to be tested.

authors: Sida Liu,Feijiang Han,Sarah Wiegreffe,Furong Huang
title: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
abstract: Finding human-interpretable directions in language-model activations is important for understanding and controlling model behavior. These directions are usually discovered through indirect learning objectives such as sparse reconstruction, but it remains unclear what existing statistical structure distinguishes interpretable directions and whether that structure can be used directly for feature discovery. We find that non-Gaussianity provides such a signature: projection distributions of natural-text residual-stream activations along sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder directions are substantially more non-Gaussian than those along random directions, with most contexts forming a concentrated background and recurring patterns often occupying one tail. This raises a natural question: if interpretable directions tend to have non-Gaussian projection distributions, can we discover them by searching for non-Gaussian directions directly in activation space, without training another sparse dictionary? To test this hypothesis, we introduce ICA Lens, a practical workflow for efficient discovery, reliable annotation, and faithful evaluation of non-Gaussian directions in LLM residual-stream activations. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, we find that: (1) the recovered non-Gaussian directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns under both human and LLM-based evaluation; (2) non-Gaussianity is positively associated with both human-label confidence and automated interpretability; and (3) the resulting coordinates are competitive with SAEs across interpretability, sparse reconstruction, concept prediction, and targeted probe perturbation, while fitting in minutes per layer and using 7-43 times less memory. These results show that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable and useful structure in activations.

authors: Hui Zhang
title: MedEvoEval: Evaluating Continual Evolution of Doctor Agents through Simulated Clinical Episodes
abstract: Doctor agents are moving beyond single-turn answer generation toward evolving clinical decision systems that acquire evidence within episodes and reuse experience across episodes. Fixed-input medical QA and many interactive benchmarks provide limited support for evaluating how episode-level decisions interact with cross-episode experience. We introduce MedEvoEval, an executable longitudinal evaluation framework based on action-gated simulated outpatient episodes. Each case is converted into role-specific patient, examination, and manager views; evidence is revealed through valid actions, and structured traces link observations, actions, final outputs, scores, and optional experience write-back. Experiments show that these traces expose process costs hidden by final-answer scoring, characterize how MDT-style consultation reallocates resources, and support analyses of memory maturation, held-out transfer, update-stage response, and backward retention. On 200 held-out cases, the mature-memory condition with sequential write-back reduces interaction turns by 0.915 and improves composite utility by 0.0483 after Holm correction. MedEvoEval provides a concrete basis for evaluating experience-driven improvement, transfer, and retention. The accompanying artifact provides 700 processed episode records with provenance, role-specific schemas, and execution, scoring, and analysis code.

authors: Filippo Ruffini,Marco Salmé,Rosa Sicilia,Valerio Guarrasi,Paolo Soda
title: SHOVIR: A Benchmark for Evaluating Vision Shortcut Learning in Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Current evaluation protocols for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in Radiology Report Generation (RRG) rely on report-level metrics that measure lexical overlap or aggregate clinical correctness. However, such metrics do not test whether individual diagnostic statements stem from the actual pathological evidence visible in the image. This allows models to achieve competitive scores by exploiting learned priors or spurious correlations, a failure mode we refer to as vision shortcut. We introduce SHOVIR, a benchmark for evaluating vision shortcut behavior in RRG. SHOVIR extends two spatially annotated chest X-ray datasets, MIMIC-CXR and PadChest-GR, with per-box CheXpert labels, and defines image-level and disease-level occlusion experiments that contrast baseline performance on clean images against localized, region-specific perturbations. Comparing predictions across these conditions isolates two failure modes at the disease-class level: direct shortcuts, where a finding persists after its visual evidence is removed, and contextual shortcuts, where detection degrades once co-occurring pathologies are occluded despite the target region remaining intact. Benchmarking eight state-of-the-art VLMs, we find that shortcut behavior varies substantially across architectures and datasets. Models achieving the highest baseline report quality do not necessarily rank highest in spatial grounding, revealing that clinically fluent generation can coexist with shallow reliance on visual evidence. These findings expose a blind spot in current RRG evaluation and motivate region-aware assessment protocols.

authors: Kwan Soo Shin
title: Arithmetic and its remedies select the evidence on learned geometry
abstract: Intelligence that must act before outside correction arrives must carry the structure of its expert knowledge, and hyperbolic geometry represents hierarchy with a fidelity no Euclidean space of comparable dimension matches. Yet hyperbolic language models confine that geometry to adapters or rebuild the transformer, and an independent audit of released hyperbolic vision language checkpoints finds their hierarchy mechanisms inactive, which has been read as evidence about the geometry or its objective. Here we show that it is also evidence about arithmetic. The constraint defining the manifold is a difference of two terms that grow together; for the unclamped map at unit curvature and temperature it fails in every format we measured, double precision included, at the norms standard language models produce in their deepest layers, beyond the limit previously derived. A common remedy, a norm bound, leaves the executed map no radial sensitivity where it acts. In a prespecified test, a tighter bound cost a Lorentz system more of the held out structure it started with than a flat one. Structural supervision has run in six expert systems over 20,951,552 training exposures. In paired runs with a published recipe's objective held fixed, removing its starting scale remedy prevented every update and removing its single precision regions raised the radius reached early in training. Arithmetic bounds the computable region, and within it, alongside the objective, arithmetic and its remedies select which runs leave a record and the states they reach on the way, so a flat surviving checkpoint cannot by itself establish that the geometry is inert.

authors: Muhammad Junaid Ali,Smail Niar,El-Ghazali Talbi
title: Multi-Objective Structured Pruning of LLMs for Latency and Model Size Optimization
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption because of their strong reasoning and query-response capabilities. However, deploying them in embedded and edge computing environments remains challenging because of strict latency, memory, and energy constraints. Their large parameter counts and computational demands hinder efficient execution on resource-constrained platforms. Although model pruning has emerged as a viable solution for reducing scale while preserving performance, jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) dimensions remains highly complex. Exhaustively exploring this combined design space is computationally expensive and often leads to local optima or unstable configurations. To address these limitations, we propose a hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. The proposed two-stage method explicitly targets latency and model size for efficient deployment on edge devices. In the coarse-grained stage, multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks to reduce computational load and memory usage. In the subsequent fine-grained stage, Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) searches for the optimal layer-wise pruning ratios for pruning under latency constraints, while importance-based strategies rank the specific components to be pruned within each layer's allocated budget. Experimental results show that our approach reduces model complexity with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning tasks and zero-shot performance. Our method achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making it suitable for edge deployment. Across multiple LLMs at 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the proposed approach achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.

authors: Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen
title: WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning
abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of large language models (LLMs). Static structured pruning is hardware-friendly, but its input-agnostic computation allocation often degrades model quality at high sparsity. Dynamic pruning adapts computation to individual tokens, but coarse-grained layer-level routing limits allocation flexibility, and finer-grained decisions introduce irregular execution that can offset computational savings. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable framework that combines token-wise structured dynamic width pruning with GPU kernel co-design for both prefill and decoding. WIDE uses differentiable routers to select GQA-aligned query-head groups and GPU-tile-aligned FFN-channel groups for each token. To execute these decisions efficiently, it reorders routing masks to cluster active tokens within each group, enabling hardware-agnostic block-level skipping and architecture-aware skipping of inactive loads and tensor-core operations. Experiments on the Llama3 and Qwen3 families demonstrate improved quality retention over representative static and dynamic pruning methods. At 50\% target routing sparsity, WIDE improves Llama3.1-8B average zero-shot accuracy by up to 20.26 points over the strongest dynamic-depth baseline under calibration-only settings, while retaining 97.6\%/88.2\% of dense Qwen3-14B likelihood/generation performance after LoRA tuning. Separate latency benchmarks demonstrate end-to-end speedups of up to $1.68\times$ for prefill and $1.55\times$ for decoding over the dense baseline. These results demonstrate that pruning--kernel co-design pushes the frontier of token-wise dynamic structured pruning, combining improved quality retention with practical acceleration across both prefill and decoding. Our code is avaliable at \url{this https URL}.

authors: Lekang Jiang,Bohan Tang,Stephan Goetz,Yiwen Guo
title: ADIAS: Automated Design of Interactive Agentic Systems
abstract: Self-evolving agents can improve without updating model weights by iteratively optimizing the harness based on evaluation feedback. Existing methods are largely candidate-centric: they record evolution outcomes (which agent variants have been produced and how they perform), rather than evolution progress (which issues, i.e., recurring failure patterns, have been fixed and which remain). Such methods pose two difficulties for cumulative harness evolution. First, repair context is scattered across candidate records and must be reconstructed every round, which leads to inefficient, redundant, or misdirected revisions. Second, because candidates are evaluated as a whole, partial fixes across different agents are difficult to combine, while ineffective changes persist alongside beneficial ones. To address these problems, we formulate issue-centric agent optimization, which explicitly carries forward evolutionary progress through a persistent issue state. We instantiate this paradigm in ADIAS, a harness-evolution framework with two key components. An Issue Manager maintains the issue state with stable issue identities, lifecycle status, supporting evidence, and intervention-outcome histories. An Issue-Guided Optimizer proposes repair targets from the issue state and performs focused harness revision. On five interactive benchmarks, ADIAS outperforms the strongest baseline by 25.2% on average and achieves consistent gains across four backbone models. Controlled ablations show that removing the Issue Manager or the Issue-Guided Optimizer reduces performance by up to 40.7%.

authors: Minglai Yang,Xinyu Guo,Zhengliang Shi,Utkarsh Tyagi,Mian Zhang,Razvan Dumitru,Sunjie Hou,Yunzhong He,Daniel Yue Zhang,Ying Liu,Dan Roth
title: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL
abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning, in which an LLM judge scores responses against prompt-specific criteria, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks without verifiable answers. The rubric, however, is only a proxy for response quality, and a policy trained against it long enough learns to exploit the difference. We train models with GRPO on medical and science rubrics and grade their responses on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks throughout training with two judges: the training judge and a stronger OOD judge. The two scores first rise together and then diverge. The policy is learning to satisfy the training judge without writing better responses, which is a form of reward hacking. To mitigate it, we propose Rubric Dropout, which applies dropout to rubric criteria: at each training step, a random subset of each rubric's criteria is removed from the reward, so the rewarded subset of criteria is resampled at each step. All responses sampled for the same prompt are scored on the same subset, so their rewards remain comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. We also introduce Block Dropout, which drops semantically similar criteria together so that a near duplicate of a dropped criterion cannot keep rewarding the same behavior. Across both benchmarks and models from 1.7B to 8B, dropout improves the gold judge's score on OOD benchmarks by up to 3 percent on HealthBench-Hard and 7 percent on ResearchQA, and it reduces both the gap between the two judges and over-crediting. It keeps in-domain reward close to the baseline, and dropout rates of 30-50 percent work best. Block Dropout improves the gold judge's OOD score further at the same dropout rate. Changing which criteria are rewarded at each step is a simple, inexpensive way to make rubric rewards harder to exploit.

authors: Guiv Farmanfarmaian
title: Selection, Recombination, or a Fresh Solve? A Candidate-Free Control for Single-Pass Test-Time Aggregation
abstract: An aggregation pass gives a language model two things: candidate solutions and another chance to answer. We ask whether the candidates improve that attempt, and whether aggregation improves on selecting an existing answer. Our candidate-free control asks the same model to solve the problem again from the problem alone, using the same decoding settings and maximum output-token allowance. On AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 reaches 15.5% accuracy when all four candidates are wrong, compared with 27.7% for a fresh solve. When at least two candidates are correct, the ordering reverses: 88.7% for aggregation versus 59.7% for a fresh solve. With exactly one correct candidate, the benefit remains unresolved under the specified test. Yet plurality voting reaches 96.0% in the multiple-correct regime without another model generation; its accuracy difference from aggregation is inconclusive (raw $p = 0.180$). The all-wrong accuracy loss and multiple-correct gain survive a statistical correction for adding the second benchmark, developed after data collection, and persist when fresh responses are scored by their final answers. These findings concern one 4B model, two mathematics benchmarks, and a single aggregation pass over candidates truncated at their first answer. All-wrong recovery can arise from solving the problem afresh. The fresh-solve control tests whether candidates improve accuracy. Comparing with selection asks whether the additional generation improves on an existing answer.

authors: Yiyang Feng,Biddut Sarker Bijoy,Niranjan Balasubramanian,Jiawei Zhou
title: Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can induce skills from completed tasks and reuse them later to grow more capable with experience. In practice, induced skills may transfer unreliably and can even harm the agent that retrieves them. When agent-induced skills transfer reliably across tasks remains an open question. We conduct a comprehensive and controlled study of how the way skills are induced shapes their transfer across tasks. Specifically, we compare task-level with subtask-level skill induction and text with code skill formats, the two axes along which existing methods differ. Task-level skills mostly reduce the agent's performance below its no-memory baseline while subtask-level skills raise it above on average, and text skills transfer better than code skills. To further understand our findings, we examine two complementary properties of the induced skills: specificity, which measures how closely a skill matches real tasks, and abstractness, which measures how evenly its relevance spreads across tasks. Neither property alone predicts task success, but their combined effect does, which we propose as a skill utility score. The score correlates consistently with task success when skills are transferred, and subtask-level and text skills score higher. Computing skill utility only needs the skills and task descriptions, so our score serves as a lightweight diagnostic of a skill memory for practitioners.

authors: Ibne Farabi Shihab,Joyanta Jyoti Mondal,Adria Binte Habib
title: Candidate-Label Saliency for Efficient Conformal Pruning of Text Classifiers
abstract: Recalibration can preserve conformal coverage after pruning while enlarging prediction sets and leaving more alternatives for downstream decisions. Directly searching for deletions that keep sets small is costly. We study whether a small candidate-gradient budget can approximate this search at lower cost. Candidate-Saliency Pruning (CSP) estimates the squared first-order change in two plausible labels' scores when each parameter is deleted. CSP averages these changes, combines the resulting importance with a base pruner, and selects the mixing weight under validation accuracy and coverage requirements. Independent split-conformal calibration supplies marginal coverage under exchangeability. We evaluate CSP on three classification tasks, two base pruners, and three sparsity levels against a squared true-label control that separates candidate choice from gradient squaring, under fixed recovery updates, equal total time, and restricted access to the training corpus. Before recovery, CSP reduces mean set size by 13.2\% to 19.2\% against the reference pruner and by 7.7\% to 13.2\% against the control in all six encoder cells at 50\% sparsity. The advantage over the control shrinks with recovery to practical equivalence in all six cells at 1,000 updates, and at equal total time the cheaper reference pruner is practically equivalent in 18 of 18 settings. When recovery is limited to the retained pruning pool, CSP keeps a meaningful advantage in all six cells. Its value therefore depends on the time and data available for recovery.

authors: Irem Yoldas,Jie Zhang,Odinaldo Rodrigues,Martim Brandão,
title: LLM-Driven Autonomous Vehicles Can Inherit Human Driver Biases in Pedestrian Yielding: Results and Implications From a New Benchmark
abstract: Public trust in Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) may depend not only on technical success but also on the fairness of their decision making. While a recent trend in AV research involves using general purpose "common sense" models to guide AV decision making, the degree to which these inherit human biases in driving is still understudied. Given that psychology studies have shown human driver biases exist, such as lower pedestrian-yielding rates to Black pedestrians in the US, we argue that analyses of model bias should also be part of AV evaluation. Concretely, in this paper we propose two new bias testing methodologies for Large Language Models (LLMs) and Visual-Language Models (VLMs), "All Else Being Equal" tests and "Self-Consistency" tests, and a new benchmark (FairYield) to assess bias in pedestrian-yielding decisions. Our findings show that the yielding decisions of both LLMs and VLMs can be influenced by models' predictions of pedestrian gender, ethnicity, religion, disability, age, skin tone, and socio-economic status. While the type and degree of bias is different from model to model, we highlight common patterns, and raise questions about the "common sense" model paradigm, particularly the need to either revise the paradigm or address issues of downstream bias.

authors: Ruoxi Shang,Christina-Maria Androna,Orfeas Menis Mastromichalakis,Yu Feng,Aniruddhan Ramesh,Rico Angell,Shang Hong Sim,Chrysoula Zerva,Emmanouil Koukoumidis
title: AURA-Eval: Evaluation Framework for Acting Under Risk Awareness in LLM Agent Trajectories
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly taking actions with real consequences, yet safety evaluations often reduce their behavior to a final safe/unsafe outcome, obscuring whether the agent recognized the risk and how it responded. We introduce AURA-Eval, a framework for evaluating whether agents recognize contextual risk and adapt their behavior accordingly. AURA-Eval truncates tool-use trajectories at safety-critical decision points and asks the evaluated model to generate the next thought and action. It creates controlled scenario variations along six risk mechanisms: harm intensity, scale, target susceptibility, system dependency, oversight, and reversibility. It also creates paired scenarios that preserve the underlying goal but differ in whether safe fulfillment is available, allowing unsafe compliance and over-refusal to be evaluated together. An LLM-judge panel, validated against human annotations, evaluates each continuation along three axes: risk detection from the reasoning trace, and action type and safety from the action. From 157 R-Judge seed trajectories, we construct 1,249 evaluation items and evaluate 20 frontier, open-weight, and safety-tuned models. Across all 20 models, unsafe-action rates are higher when no safe path for request fulfillment is available than when one is; for frontier models, the rates are 27-40% versus 5-7%. When a safe path exists, frontier models rarely refuse; when none exists, they most often propose an alternative. Open-weight models, by contrast, more often execute the request than propose alternatives and act unsafely on 58-83% of items. Controlled risk-mechanism analyses further show particularly high unsafe rates under changes to oversight and scale; removing pre-execution oversight flips 52.3% of cases that were safe on the corresponding original scenario to unsafe.

authors: Youngrok Park,Sangmin Bae,Hojung Jung,Jongwoo Ko,Yunseon Choi,Young Jin Kim,Pashmina Cameron,Aaron Courville,Se-Young Yun
title: Eliciting Weak-to-Strong Generalization with On-Policy Reverse Distillation
abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether stronger models can learn from weaker supervisors and surpass them. This is particularly important for successive model generations and multi-domain consolidation, where frontier-scale post-training from scratch can be prohibitively expensive. Yet conventional distillation treats the weak teacher as an optimization target, potentially imposing its capacity ceiling on the student. We introduce On-Policy Reverse Distillation (OPRD), which evaluates the teacher's policy shift relative to its reference policy on student rollouts and amplifies the component of the student's verifier-driven policy gradient along that direction. By rescaling only verifier-supported updates, OPRD preserves the stationary points of policy optimization while accelerating learning beyond the teacher. Our evaluations cover mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, code generation, and visual tool use. In both successive model transfer and multi-teacher distillation, OPRD achieves higher performance with fewer student updates than existing RL and distillation approaches. Response-style analysis shows that OPRD students remain closer to verifier-only RL models than to their weak teachers, suggesting that guidance accelerates rather than redirects student optimization. Strong-to-weak results further show that OPRD combines verifier-driven optimization with teacher guidance regardless of capacity ordering.

authors: Andre Bacellar
title: Predictable Failure in Multi-Hop Retrieval: Score-Distributional Confidence Scoring and Abstention
abstract: Multi-hop retrieval failures are not uniformly distributed across queries: they cluster in structurally predictable subpopulations. We prove two results formalizing this structure. First (CWAR Reducibility): confident-failure reduction is achievable if and only if retrieval features carry mutual information about success, a condition satisfied by LLM-judge pipelines but substantially weaker in dense-only settings, explaining the AUC-AC gap between regimes. Second (Feature Regime Complementarity): no single ANN score feature achieves best predictive performance across all failure regimes; the dominant feature differs between datasets (query length on MuSiQue, hop-1 concentration on HoVer), and a constructive witness pair shows each is necessary in one regime and non-contributory in the other. We instantiate these principles in RegimeAbstain, which computes a Retrieval Confidence Score (RCS), a logistic function of up to nine query-ANN structural features, all available without any additional LLM call, and uses it to implement a calibrated abstention policy. We define the Confident-Wrong-Answer Rate (CWAR) metric and evaluate across three multi-hop benchmarks (MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HoVer) and two retrieval architectures (LLM-judge and dense-only), covering five failure regimes with CWAR from 14.5% to 62.1%. RCS achieves best or co-best AUC-AC in all five conditions against eight confidence baselines. On MuSiQue (LLM-judge), RCS reduces CWAR from 39.5% to 20.6% at 50% coverage (47.8% relative reduction), with ECE=0.035. A model trained on MuSiQue transfers to 2WikiMultiHopQA with only -0.5pp AUC loss, confirming the domain-agnostic structure of regime features.

authors: Xiangxi Tian,Ran Guan
title: Toollery: Scaling LLM Agents to Thousands of Skills and Tools
abstract: As LLM agents are exposed to hundreds to tens of thousands of skills, tools, and API functions, full-library prompting becomes costly, slow, and less reliable: each added candidate increases prompt tokens and latency, while longer candidate lists introduce more distractors for LLM selection. We present Toollery, a training-free candidate-compression framework for scalable LLM skill/tool selection. Following established document-side query expansion, Toollery generates user-intent queries from each skill/tool specification and builds a retrieval index that maps real user requests to compact candidate sets before final LLM decision-making. By treating high-level skills and atomic tools as selectable capabilities, Toollery can be applied to both skill libraries and tool registries. We evaluate Toollery on the roughly 79K-capability SkillRouter benchmark, BFCL-V4 with over 440 atomic tools, and 3,396 proprietary smart-cockpit requests over 220 tools. Across these settings, Toollery keeps online selection bounded to a compact top-K candidate set and improves recall over ordinary specification retrieval. At a fixed top-10 budget, Toollery improves end-to-end selection on the cockpit dataset, and maintains comparable AST Accuracy on BFCL-V4. These results support Toollery as a practical candidate-compression framework for large and evolving agent capability libraries, while showing that quality and cost gains depend on workload coverage and provider caching.

authors: Ming Ma,Yi Zhu,Yiran Zhong,Feida Zhu,Chonghan Liu,Pengkun Jiao,Qichao Wang,Yanhao Jia,Tianming Yang,Steven Hoi
title: ProCredit: From Outcome Rewards to Progress Credit in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require an agent to modify an environment through a sequence of tool calls, with success determined by the final state. The standard recipe assigns a single outcome reward at the end and compares trajectories sampled for the same task. As a result, a group with no successful trajectory yields no training signal, failed attempts cannot be told apart by how close they came to completion, and turns that advance the task receive the same credit as turns that only query the environment. Prior work refines the unit of comparison from the trajectory to the step, or trains a reward model to supply intermediate signal: the former still derives its signal from final success alone, and the latter estimates it with a model. We observe that the acceptance checks that decide success can also be run on intermediate states, so progress is as verifiable as the outcome. We propose ProCredit, which turns this verified progress into credit: it reruns the acceptance checks after each turn, rewards the turn by its change in progress, and uses these rewards to assign credit both across attempts at the same task and across the turns within a trajectory. Starting from Qwen3.5 base models at three scales on AppWorld, ProCredit outperforms outcome-reward baselines and progress-based baselines in task completion rate at every scale on both test sets, exceeding the strongest outcome-reward baseline by 4.1 percentage points at 4B, and results in a second environment show the same direction of improvement. Ablations show that adding the final progress to the trajectory score alone does not improve performance: the gain comes from crediting progress to the turn where it occurs.

authors: Seunghan Lee,Jun Seo,Jaehoon Lee,Junhyeok Kang,Sangjun Han,Sungdong Yoo,Minjae Kim,Tae Yoon Lim,Dongwan Kang,Hwanil Choi,Soonyoung Lee,Wonbin Ahn
title: PALM: Point-in-Time Adaptation for Financial Language Models
abstract: Language models used in financial backtests suffer from look-ahead bias, as a model trained on text published after the study period has already observed the outcomes it is asked to predict. To handle this issue, point-in-time (PIT) language models are pretrained on chronologically filtered corpora and released as one checkpoint per calendar year, each with a documented cutoff. However, each additional year costs another pretraining run, and whether that run is necessary has never been tested. In this paper, we show that a newer checkpoint is not detectably better on the decision it informs, as its information coefficient on a fixed evaluation window shows no decay with age that we can detect. Motivated by this observation, we propose PALM (Point-in-time Adaptation for financial Language Models), a simple yet effective alternative to annual pretraining that fits a low-rank adapter on financial text the checkpoint is allowed to read, without modifying any pretrained weight. We further find that the gain comes from the financial domain rather than from recency, which leaves the point-in-time constraint without a detectable cost. We validate PALM on a decade of financial news and on three families of PIT models, whose cutoffs span two decades. The pooled gain keeps its sign across experimental settings and comes at a small fraction of the cost of pretraining. Code is available at:this https URL.

authors: Ali Holmov,Yiran Huang,Kirill Bykov,Zeynep Akata
title: User Model Extraction via Belief Self-Distillation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) implicitly infer attributes of their users and adapt their behavior accordingly, yet these beliefs remain difficult to inspect and causally manipulate. We introduce Belief Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified read-write framework that bridges linear and causal probing by learning a compact user representation that can be both decoded and written back into the model. The frozen LLM acts as its own teacher, distilling beliefs from natural conversations without external annotations. Unlike conventional probing, BSD isolates not only information present in activations, but a state whose causal role can be directly tested. Across multiple model families, BSD faithfully recovers user beliefs and enables substantially stronger interventions than matched hidden-state steering. Crucially, we find that refusal depends not only on the request, but on the model's inferred user intent: changing this belief alters refusal while holding the request fixed. We further uncover a striking cross-model regularity: independently trained LLMs converge on a shared geometry for representing their users. Together, these results reveal implicit user models as readable and causally writable internal states with direct implications for AI safety, shaping how models condition safety decisions on whom they believe they are interacting with.

authors: Michael Kirchhof,Eleonora Gualdoni,Andrew Szot,Khashayar Gatmiry,Aryo Lotfi,Abbas Kazerouni,Omar Attia,Sanjoy Chowdhury,Alexander Toshev
title: RLTLDR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback
abstract: The common paradigm of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is to let agents make multiple attempts at a task, and optimize towards the successful ones. This becomes problematic in the realms of self-improvement, where tasks are so difficult that the agent has a low or even no chance of success, and where there are no teacher models or example solutions to distill from. In this paper, we introduce RLTLDR. After each failed attempt, we show the policy the verifier outputs and let it write its own feedback, in the form of a single TL;DR insight. The next rollout is conditioned on all previous insights, and we sequentially sample rollouts until a solution is found. Moreover, we enable backpropagation on the in-context insights to internalize a direct task to insight mapping. On challenging tool-calling and coding datasets (filtered to Pass@128=0), standard GRPO training of a Qwen 3.5 9B Thinking policy stays flat at a Pass@1 of 0% to 1%. RLTLDR breaks through this learning barrier, achieving a Pass@1 of 14-31% with insights in context during training and, crucially, 12-13% when no insight is in context at eval time. We identify that the key is the task to insight internalization. To study this further, we reduce our approach to SFTLDR, training only on (task, insight) tuples, without showing or backpropagating on any rollouts. Training on only 4k of these tuples recovers almost the full performance of RLTLDR and classical SFT on full rollouts. This demonstrates a promising compacted training paradigm of the form "on this sort of task, keep this sort of thing in mind", which we hope to inspire future research on.

authors: Chun-Wah Hsu,Kai Gong,Yu Wu,Xianhe Chen,Mengyang Liu,Jie Li,Hanyu Li,Zhixuan Liu,Naisheng Tang,Jiaying Chi,Ziheng Fan,Xuning He,Xiaokang Yang,Xue Jiang,Yihong Dong
title: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration and controlled causal evaluation.

authors: Orion Reblitz-Richardson
title: Principled Under Pressure: Post-Training Decides Whether LLMs Act on Their Own Moral Judgment
abstract: An agent that can say an action is wrong and then take it anyway is a different failure from one that does not know better, and evaluations of stated values cannot see it. We ask how often open models act against their own moral judgment under pressure, and what decides and reduces it. We build a pre-registered panel of 248 scenarios across five kinds of pressure. Each scenario is posed to one model in two separate calls, as the agent choosing among fixed options and in the third person asking which is right; the model's own judgment is the reference, and the scenario's construction fixes which option counts as the violation. Every scenario has a twin with the pressure removed, and every model gets a positive control that bounds what the instrument can see. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, the model takes the action it judged wrong on one in five of the scenarios screened on its own actions, more often than with the pressure removed. Whether the gap appears depends on the post-training recipe: OLMo-3 and Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct carry it; Tulu 3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OpenAI's GPT-OSS-20B, read without reasoning, show none within stated detection bars. Meta's recipe and Ai2's Tulu 3 share the same Llama-3.1 weights; only Meta's carries the gap. On both models that carry it, reasoning about the stakes before acting moves the choice back toward the model's own judgment. What that deliberation tracks is the stated rule: where following a written rule harms an absent third party, it still moves OLMo-3 and GPT-OSS-20B toward the rule, not detectably diminished, while Llama-3.1's brake shrinks to about a seventh. Whether a model acts on its own moral judgment is therefore not settled by pretraining, and deliberation moves the action toward the stated rule, which protects people only when the rule does. The gap is a measurable target for post-training recipes, not a fixed property of the model.

authors: Huishan Ji,Weiming Zhang,Qirui Ye,Jinchao Xu,Yike Guo,Hua Xu
title: EdgeRock: Strong Reasoning at Constant Memory
abstract: We present EdgeRock, a family of multimodal models that deliver strong reasoning at constant memory. Most models keep reasoning history in a key-value (KV) cache that grows with every token, consuming accelerator memory, limiting concurrent requests, and competing with perception and control on edge devices. With fixed history, memory is allocated once and never runs out, however long the model reasons. Constant memory alone is not new: bounded-state models (recurrent, state-space, and sliding-window) already achieve it, but often at the cost of reasoning, because they cannot keep the distant details that later reasoning needs. We therefore introduce Rock Memory Anchors (RMA): the model learns what is worth remembering and stores it as KV records in a fixed-size bank, directly readable however far back the source lies. EdgeRock-4B, our first open-source release, supports text and image reasoning and reaches 82.9% mean pass@1 on AIME 2024-2026, while the bounded-state models we evaluate reach at most 18.8%, even at 14B scale. This result is on par with leading compact models whose memory grows with reasoning. Compared with its source model, EdgeRock-4B uses up to 99.1% less KV cache and delivers up to 6.42$\times$ higher end-to-end batch throughput.

authors: Sergei Katkov,Antonio Liotta
title: Understanding Personalization Gains in Whisper ASR
abstract: Whisper-style ASR models provide strong zero-shot transcription, but their residual errors are not evenly distributed across datasets, recording conditions, and metadata-based groups. We study when lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves Whisper and whether observed gains require group-specific adapters. Across Common Voice, LibriSpeech, and VoxPopuli, we compare zero-shot Whisper, pooled LoRA, and group-specific LoRA under matched within-group splits. We find that adaptation is not uniformly beneficial: gains are concentrated in difficult Common Voice groups, are consistent on VoxPopuli, and largely disappear on low-error LibriSpeech. Crucially, pooled LoRA often matches, and sometimes clearly outperforms, group-specific LoRA. Gains over zero-shot should therefore be tested against matched pooled adaptation before being interpreted as evidence of personalization.

authors: Muyao Kong,Zhihao Lin
title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.

authors: Kyusong Lee,Heting Ying,Tiancheng Zhao
title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present VLX-GO, a vision-language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces. Code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Qianru Meng,Xi Zhang,Konstantinos Papakostas,Congfeng Cao,Wenxiang Hu,Tianyi Lu,Xiao Zhang,Lun Zhou,Zaiqiao Meng,Zhaochun Ren,Xiaohui Yan,Yougang Lyu
title: SwarmRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Scientific Agent Swarm
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) in scientific research aims to improve agents' research capabilities through their own experimental experience. Scientific agent swarms can combine evidence and implementations from different research directions to guide their agents' subsequent experiments. However, poor experimental results can leave unclear whether to revise a hypothesis or its implementation, while overall program scores can hide components useful to other agents. To address these challenges, we introduce SwarmRSI, a framework that evolves scientific agent swarms for recursive self-improvement. We devise Feedback-Guided Swarm Mutation to refine hypotheses and their implementations using experimental feedback from other agents. We also propose Complementary Swarm Recombination to reuse retained hypotheses and complementary program components across agents, allowing partial results to support new research. Recursive Swarm Evolution integrates both mechanisms into a feedback loop, using new experimental evidence to guide subsequent research. Experiments on OpenProblems, NatureBench and MLE-Bench Lite demonstrate SwarmRSI's state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. Further evaluations show that accumulated research experience improves performance on held-out tasks. Biologists also reproduce its programs for follow-up biological analyses.

authors: Zhivar Sourati,Marianne Menglin Liu,Rongguang Wang,Zheng Wang,Yazhe Hu,Lan Guo,Yuying Wang,Mengqing Guo,Bhavesh Dnyaneshwar Gore,Shubham Pathak,Ramapriya Ranganath,Sandeep Sharma,Tao Sheng,Sujith Ravi,Dan Roth
title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available atthis https URL.

authors: Cassie Huang,Zhanwei Cao,Yeawon Lee,Nathalia Gomez,Zhuoyi Yang,Ian G. Harris,Tiffany D. Do,Jiayuan Mao,Li Zhang
title: Planning Commitment of LLM under Partial Observability
abstract: LLM-based planning agents commit to plans of different lengths before interacting with a partially observable environment. Some aggressively commit to a long plan based on assumptions about unobserved states, while others conservatively plan only over what they have observed. Both behaviors emerge implicitly in pre-trained models, whether the LLM outputs a plan directly or generates a PDDL formulation for a classical solver. Aggressive commitment risks costly failures, while conservative commitment risks excessive LLM calls. This choice pits safety against efficiency, a trade-off that has been neither characterized systematically nor made controllable. We investigate aggressive and conservative LLM planners and formalizers on two partially observable domains, where priors are provided as either explicit statistics or common-sense knowledge. Across three LLMs, both strategies reach similar accuracy. Conservative methods achieve fewer failed attempts (safety) at the cost of more API calls (efficiency). Aggressive methods fail more often but replan efficiently only when priors are informative. Interestingly, analysis shows that LLMs treat the provided priors nearly as facts, which risks failure when priors are unreliable. We also explore hybrid strategies with tunable hyperparameters that adjust the balance between safety and efficiency.

authors: Yutong Leng,Haojiong Chen,Fukai Shang,Xiaoyang Wang,Mindong Liu,Runyuan Ma,Jiantao Qiu
title: Do Agents Need a New Kind of Paper? SPRA: Structured Paper Representation for Agents
abstract: Scientific agents must connect research problems, methods, and findings dispersed through narrative articles. We introduce SPRA (Structured Paper Representation for Agents), a paper-level representation of persistent research objects and typed relations. Its empirical-AI profile organizes Problems, Contributions, Components, ExperimentSetups, Measures, and Findings for querying, traversal, and reuse. Selected paper-level citation relations record dependencies, component use, and comparisons with prior work; source locations support verification. We instantiate SPRA across more than one million AI papers, with 19.95 million research units and 24.07 million internal relations. Evaluations access SPRA through Schema-RAG with task evidence fixed before inference. Across seven subfields, SPRA improves source-conditioned scientific QA by 0.381/5 over passage retrieval while remaining close to Full Compact (0.078/5 lower on average). In directed cross-paper reasoning, qualification improves by 0.184/5 over passage retrieval; Top-5 synthesis shows mixed quality effects. Across all paired RQ2 tasks, including Top-5, input+output tokens decrease by 28.5% relative to passage retrieval and 95.3% relative to Full Compact. In idea generation, a 0.067-point lower Overall score than Full Compact accompanies 93.7% fewer input+output tokens. Together, these results support SPRA as a usable representation of scientific content and a foundation for research workflows that connect, inspect, and reuse paper-level research objects. The SPRA resource is accessible through the Sciverse scholarly-data platform.

authors: Yanchen Deng,Jianguo Huang,Yao Long Teng,Yixuan Li,Handuo Zhang,Ning Wang,Liangcai Su,Xinyu Wang,Bo An
title: HTN-Orchestrate: A Hierarchical Task Network Framework for Multi-Agent Orchestration
abstract: Orchestrating multiple agents on a complex task requires reconciling local subtask execution with global task planning. Dynamic dispatch approaches provide execution flexibility but do not explicitly model subtask hierarchies or dependencies, while predefined workflows impose this structure but fix the decomposition before execution begins. Therefore, we introduce HTN-Orchestrate, a two-layer framework that separates these responsibilities through a hierarchical task network (HTN). The Planner maintains subtask hierarchies and dependencies, deferring decomposition until prerequisite results become available, while local Orchestrators schedule workers to execute each leaf subtask. Results propagate upward under \textbf{AND} semantics, and accumulated findings inform a rebuilt task network when the current decomposition cannot resolve the task. On five benchmarks spanning web research, scientific reasoning, and research workflows, HTN-Orchestrate outperforms ReAct, Agent Team, and DeepSeek Harness using the same base model, achieving 89.73% accuracy on BrowseComp and 73.44% on SUPERChem, exceeding Agent Team by 2.45 and 4.69 percentage points, respectively.

authors: Guowei Xu,Zhenting Qi,Amani Kiruga,Himabindu Lakkaraju,Yilun Du
title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. More details are available on our project page atthis https URL.

authors: Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj,Chenyi Huang,Bin Wu,Sahan Bulathwela
title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.

authors: Md Sajid,Shreeyut Maheshwari,Akshat Mishra,Ritik Mishra,Mohammad Tanveer
title: I$^2$-Med: Interpretable Medical Inference through Visual-Guided Dynamic Logits Calibration
abstract: Medical vision language models have demonstrated strong potential for medical image understanding and reasoning. However, their interpretability and reliability remain limited because medical vision language tasks require precise visual grounding and clinically coherent explanations. This is particularly challenging due to complex imaging patterns and scarce expert annotations. These challenges reduce the effectiveness of conventional reasoning methods and lead to visual hallucination, defined as the generation of text that is not grounded in the given visual input, which further limits their applicability in clinical practice. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an interpretable medical inference (I$^2$-Med) framework that enhances visual faithfulness during inference without additional training to improve reasoning and explanation faithfulness in medical vision language models. During text generation, I$^2$-Med uses a visual guidance module to check whether each candidate word is supported by the medical image and consistent with the current reasoning. Based on this guidance, the model's output scores are adjusted to favor visually grounded words, without changing the model parameters. Extensive experiments on the OmniMedVQA benchmark, covering eight medical imaging modalities and five clinical question types, demonstrate that our proposed I$^2$-Med framework generates more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces visual hallucination under standard medical VQA evaluation metrics. The source code is publicly available at \url{this https URL}.

authors: Cai Ke,Xinghao Chen,Yuanchen Bei,Yuni Lai,Keyu Chen,Ruizhi Qiao,Siyu An,Junnan Dong,Ruifeng Xu,Xing Sun
title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.

authors: Ruochen Zhao,Jiazheng Kang,Gezi Li,Dongying Lin,Ting Bai
title: EMMA: Event-Driven Multimodal Memory System with Multi-Agent Retrieval
abstract: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available atthis https URL.

authors: Aleksandr Druzhinin
title: Path-Conditioned Attention Mobility: From Depth to Execution Hubs in SegFormer
abstract: Transformer compression often couples two distinct quantities: retained attention capacity and the number of sequential depths at which that capacity is executed. We study whether useful attention functions in a hierarchical vision transformer are locally mobile across depth. Using SegFormer-B5 for human segmentation, we find that some task-relevant attention heads can be relocated to nearby depths, but only when their computational context is respected. Head-only relocation is insufficient, while joint adaptation of the relocated head and surrounding representation boundary improves functional preservation; replacing donor-specific normalization and spatial-reduction preprocessing causes large degradation. We use this path-conditioned mobility to reorganize retained attention from depth into width. Starting from a fixed parent with 120 retained Stage-3 heads across 40 attention execution depths, we consolidate the same 120-head budget into 20 execution hubs. Under a layout-matched three-seed recovery control, K20 reaches 0.960686 +/- 0.000059 mIoU versus 0.960400 +/- 0.000074 for the corresponding State120 control. The paired point difference is +0.000285, while a paired image-bootstrap confidence interval includes zero; we therefore interpret the result as no measurable quality penalty rather than statistical superiority. For deployment, FOLDED_VEC preserves donor-specific paths while vectorizing their execution. Relative to the same 120-head State120 parent, it reduces end-to-end NVIDIA L4 latency by 5.28%, 3.15%, and 3.58% at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8. These results suggest that attention redundancy includes not only removable capacity but also execution-depth redundancy, provided that the computational path defining a relocated function is preserved.

authors: Yiming Shu,Peng Sun,Lang Zhang,Mingyue Feng,Yaonong Wang,Pei Liu,Chen Sun,Jun Ma
title: GeoForward: Geometry-Guided Cross-View Alignment for Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an {appearance-driven paradigm}: multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. However, calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, \textbf{Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction}, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce \textbf{GeoForward}. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction.

authors: Siddharth Viswanath,Hiren Madhu,Eddie Cavallin,Benjamin Jones,Alistair Wilkinson,Christopher Tape,Michael Perlmutter,Rex Ying,Ian Adelstein,Smita Krishnaswamy
title: RhinoNet: Unsupervised Learning for Phenoscaping and Generation of High Dimensional Point Clouds
abstract: We present RhinoNet, a simplicial complex-based point cloud neural network, that creates a geometry-preserving embedding of high-dimensional point clouds. RhinoNet takes collections of datasets, also called {\em data cohorts}, and processes each dataset (point cloud) within the cohort as a simplicial complex. These simplicial complexes have datapoints as vertices and edges learned by Vietoris-Rips filtration. Using simplicial wavelets and MLP layers, RhinoNet computes a vector representation of each dataset in a latent space produced by an autoencoder. The latent space is optimized such that an optimal transport distance between pairs of point clouds is preserved between the latent representations. We apply RhinoNet to single-cell datasets collected on patients---a common source of such high-dimensional data. RhinoNet creates a patient level representation, known in biological contexts as a phenoscape. We establish that RhinoNet generates organized phenoscapes, whereas other methods such as static maps do not. Next we show that we can generate entire point clouds by sampling and decoding this phenoscape. We show two modes of generation via 1) latent flow matching and 2) geodesic interpolation in latent space, followed by a decoding back into the point cloud space. RhinoNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-cell and spatial data cohorts relative to tested baselines. Overall, RhinoNet lifts the concepts of representation learning and generative modeling to the point cloud or population level and defines a neural model for phenoscaping.

authors: Naveen Stewart
title: EAGLE: Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer for Partially Polygon-Supervised Object Localization
abstract: Object detection is a critical application of computer vision, yet models trained uniformly on bounding boxes lack the geometric precision to be fully effective in inference settings, especially at high IoU thresholds.
